A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original numerical experiments, including FICO-initialized simulations, optimized threshold sequences, agent trajectories, and parameter ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original simulations and adds parameter-misspecification, binary-comparator, alternative-dynamics, and numerical-sensitivity results.

M1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds explicit model variants with nonlinearly level-dependent leg-up bonuses and a corresponding threshold construction, beyond v1's implemented linear bonus. The core ternary mechanism, greedy heuristic, and VALUEITERATE algorithm remain unchanged; the algorithms are relocated or renumbered.

E1.justification: The FICO-based initial population and credit-building task are retained. Added simulations extend scenario coverage to mismatched principal beliefs and true agent parameters, and to constant, square-root, and logarithmic leg-up dynamics.

E2.justification: Appendix E.5 adds an evaluated binary promote-or-relegate comparator without the stay option. Figure 16 compares it with the ternary mechanism after optimizing both with CMA-ES; this comparison was absent from v1.

E3.justification: Existing experiments retain their stated settings. New protocols optimize under perturbed parameter beliefs and evaluate under true parameters, measure oracle-relative utility loss and terminal gaming, and compare binary and ternary rules under matched conditions. Additional protocols specify a 30-by-30 bound sweep and controlled grid-resolution and truncation sweeps.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained parameter ablations, v2 tests sensitivity to misspecification, dependence on leg-up shape, the contribution of abstention, restrictiveness of feasibility conditions, and numerical discretization/truncation. These additions substantially expand analysis of mechanisms, failure conditions, and numerical reliability.

E5.justification: The trajectory and improvement-fraction plots retain their mean and plus/minus one standard deviation reporting. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new parameter-error sweeps do not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 5.1 and the original plotted results are unchanged, but substantial results are added. Table 5.2 reports 82.4% utility loss and 100% terminal gaming for a +10% retention error. Figure 16 reports 0% versus 100% gaming for ternary versus binary rules around gaming costs 0.3–0.4; further additions report dynamics and numerical-sensitivity outcomes.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds formal assumptions on level-dependent bonuses and Proposition D.3, giving generalized feasibility/infeasibility conditions and a threshold construction using average bonus increments. This extends the central feasibility analysis beyond the linear case; v1 already discussed general dynamics but lacked these results. Existing main theorems and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain the same core claims: sequential incentives enlarge the incentivizable region, two-level optimal strategies can be characterized, and suitable threshold sequences enable arbitrarily high honest attainment under stated conditions. The added analyses do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains misspecification failures through overly ambitious designs and recommends conservative parameter beliefs. It newly interprets abstention as essential near the feasibility boundary and saturating bonuses as limiting attainment. It also adds a broad 30–50% misspecification-tolerance claim requiring reconciliation with the reported failures.

D1.justification: Appendix E.6 newly reports concrete numerical settings, including truncation at 30, grid step 0.05, and binary-search precision 0.05. The binary comparison also documents removing the stay branch from the Bellman operator. Existing CMA-ES population-size and iteration-budget disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Alkarmi et al. (2025) to connect abstention with deterrence of manipulation, and Huang et al. (2026) as a companion stochastic extension. The broader positioning against sequential regression, strategic classification, and self-selection research remains unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized timing and scaling clarifications, paragraph rewrites, expanded discussion, and new appendix subsections. The overall narrative remains intact. Several references to assumptions, propositions, and lemmas are newly mislabeled as theorems.

P2.justification: v2 adds the main-text misspecification table and visualizations for leg-up shapes, feasibility bounds, binary comparisons, and grid/truncation sensitivity. The greedy pseudocode moves from the appendix into Section 5.1. Existing plots retain their content despite relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: The new robustness and comparator experiments address meaningful validation gaps. However, Appendix E.4 substitutes beta times gamma squared for beta times gamma divided by two in the retained theorem's bound, and its broad tolerance claim is not reconciled with Table 5.2's severe failures. Proposition D.3 also omits the improvement-cost factor from reward bounds claimed to recover Theorem 4.2. These substantive inconsistencies offset the useful additions enough to prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
